title: Book 9
paragraphs: Lord, I am your servant; I am your servant, and the son of your servant-woman. You have broken my chains apart. I will offer you the sacrifice of praise. Let my heart and my tongue praise you; yes, let all my bones say, Lord, who is like you? Let them say it, and answer me, and say to my soul, I am your salvation. Who am I, and what am I? What evil have I not done — in deed, or if not in deed, then in word, or if not in word, then in will? But you, Lord, are good and merciful, and your right hand reached down into the depth of my death, and emptied that abyss of corruption from the bottom of my heart. And this was your whole gift: that I should stop willing what I willed, and will what you willed. But through all those years, and out of what low and deep hiding place, was my free will summoned forth in a single moment, to bend my neck to your easy yoke and my shoulders to your light burden, Christ Jesus, my helper and my redeemer? How sweet it suddenly became to me to be free of the sweetness of those trifles! What I had feared to lose was now a joy to give up. For you drove them out of me, you who are the true and highest sweetness. You drove them out, and in their place entered yourself — sweeter than every pleasure, though not to flesh and blood; brighter than every light, but more hidden than any depth; higher than all honor, but not to those who think themselves high. Now my soul was free of the biting cares of ambition and gain, of wallowing in filth and scratching at the itch of lust. And my infant tongue spoke freely to you, my brightness, my riches, and my health, the Lord my God.

And I resolved, in your sight, not to tear the service of my tongue violently away from the marketplace of word-selling, but to withdraw it gently — so that the young men who studied not your law, nor your peace, but liars' fantasies and courtroom battles, would no longer buy weapons for their madness from my mouth. And very conveniently, only a few days now remained until the Vintage Vacation, and I resolved to endure them, then take my leave in the ordinary way, and, having been bought by you, never again return for sale. Our purpose was known to you; but to anyone besides our own friends, it was not known. For we had agreed among ourselves not to let it out to anyone — though to us, now climbing up out of the valley of tears and singing that song of ascents, you had given sharp arrows and burning coals against the subtle tongue, which, as if advising us for our own good, would have opposed us, and out of a kind of love would have devoured us, as it devours its own food.

You had pierced our hearts with your love, and we carried your words fixed, as it were, in our very insides; and the examples of your servants, whom you had turned from black to bright, and from dead to living, gathered together in the storehouse of our thoughts, kindled and burned away our heavy sluggishness, so that we would not sink down into the depths; and they set us so fiercely on fire that all the gusts of clever tongues from those who argued against us could only inflame us further, not put us out. And yet, because for the sake of your name, which you have made holy throughout the earth, this vow and purpose of ours might also find people to commend it, it seemed like showing off not to wait for the vacation, now so near, but instead to give up beforehand a public position that was before everyone's eyes — so that everyone watching this act of mine, and noticing how close was the time of the vintage that I wanted to get ahead of, would talk a great deal about me, as if I had wanted to seem important. And what good would it have done me, for people to think about and argue over my purpose, and for our good to be spoken of as evil.

Moreover, it had troubled me at first that this very summer my lungs began to fail, under too much literary labor, and to struggle to draw a full breath, and to show, by the pain in my chest, that they were damaged, and to refuse any full or lengthy speaking; this had troubled me, because it almost forced me to lay down the burden of teaching, or, if I could be cured and recover, at least to suspend it for a while. But when the full desire for leisure — so that I might see how you are the Lord — arose in me and took hold, my God, you know it, I began even to rejoice that I had this second reason, and not a pretended one, which might somewhat soften the offense taken by those who, for their sons' sake, wished I would never have the freedom of your sons. Full then of this joy, I endured until that stretch of time had run out; it may have been some twenty days, yet they were endured bravely — endured, because the love of gain, which had before played some part in this heavy business, had left me, and I was left alone, and would have been overwhelmed, had not patience taken its place. Perhaps some of your servants, my brothers, will say that I sinned in this, that with a heart fully set on your service, I let myself sit even one more hour in that chair of lies. I will not argue the point. But have you not, most merciful Lord, pardoned and forgiven this sin too, along with my other most horrible and deadly sins, in the holy water?

Verecundus was worn down with worry over this happiness of ours, because he saw that, being held back by bonds that bound him most tightly, he would be cut off from us. For he himself was not yet a Christian, though his wife was one of the faithful; and it was this, more than any other chain, that held him back and hindered him from the journey we had now taken up. For he said he would not be a Christian on any terms but those he could not accept. All the same, he graciously offered to let us stay at his country house for as long as we remained there. You, Lord, will reward him at the resurrection of the just, since you have already given him the portion of the righteous. For although, in our absence, now at Rome, he was seized with a bodily sickness, and in it was made a Christian, one of the faithful, and departed this life; still you had mercy not only on him but on us as well — so that, remembering the great kindness our friend had shown us, and yet unable to count him among your flock, we should not be tormented with unbearable sorrow. Thanks to you, our God, we are yours: your promptings and your comforts tell us so. Faithful to your promises, you now repay Verecundus for his country house at Cassiciacum, where we found rest in you from the world's fever, with the everlasting freshness of your paradise — for you have forgiven him his sins on earth, on that rich mountain, that mountain flowing with milk, your own mountain.

He then had sorrow at that time, but Nebridius had joy. For although he too, not yet being a Christian, had fallen into the pit of that most dangerous error, believing the flesh of your Son to be a mere appearance, he came out of it and believed as we did — not yet admitted to any of the sacraments of your Church, but a most eager seeker after truth. Not long after our conversion and rebirth through your baptism, he too became a faithful member of the Catholic Church, serving you in perfect chastity and self-control among his own people in Africa — his whole household having through him first become Christian — and you released him from the flesh; and now he lives in Abraham's bosom. Whatever that bosom means, there my Nebridius lives, my sweet friend and your child, Lord, adopted from a freed slave: there he lives. For what other place could there be for such a soul? There he lives, asking me now for so much, the very things I, in my inexperience, used to be asked about by him. Now he no longer presses his ear to my mouth, but presses his spiritual mouth to your fountain, and drinks as much as he can hold, wisdom in proportion to his thirst, endlessly happy. And I do not think he is so drunk on it as to forget me, since you, Lord, whom he drinks, are mindful of us. So we comforted Verecundus, who grieved, as far as friendship allowed, that our conversion had come at such a cost to him; and we urged him to become one of the faithful, within his own measure, that is, as a married man; and we waited for Nebridius to follow us, which, being so close to it, he was all but doing. And so, look, those days rolled by at last — long and many as they seemed, for the love I bore to that easy freedom, that I might sing to you from the depths of my heart, My heart has said to you, I have sought your face; your face, Lord, I will seek.

Now the day had come when I was, in fact, to be freed from my professorship of rhetoric, from which in thought I was already free. And it was done. You rescued my tongue, as you had already rescued my heart. And I blessed you, rejoicing, withdrawing with my whole household to the villa. What I wrote there, work now enlisted in your service, though still, in this breathing space as it were, panting from the school of pride — my books can bear witness, both what I debated with others and what I debated with myself alone, before you; and my letters bear witness to what I discussed with Nebridius, who was absent. And when will I have time to recount all your great gifts to us in that period, especially when I am hurrying on toward even greater mercies? For my memory calls me back, and it is pleasant to me, Lord, to confess to you by what inward goads you tamed me, and how you leveled me, lowering the mountains and hills of my lofty imaginings, straightening my crookedness, and smoothing my rough ways; and how you also brought the brother of my heart, Alypius, under the name of your only-begotten Son, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ — a name he would not at first allow to be inserted into our writings. For he would rather they carried the flavor of the lofty cedars of the schools, which the Lord has now broken down, than of the wholesome herbs of the Church, the antidote against serpents.

Oh, in what tones did I speak to you, my God, when I read the Psalms of David, those faithful songs, those sounds of devotion that allow no room for a swollen spirit — still only a catechumen, and a beginner in your true love, resting at that villa, with Alypius a catechumen too, and my mother clinging to us, in a woman's body but a man's faith, with the calm of old age, a mother's love, and a Christian devotion! Oh, what tones did I utter to you in those Psalms, and how they set me on fire toward you, and made me burn to recite them, if it were possible, throughout the whole world, against the pride of mankind! And yet they are sung throughout the whole world, and no one can hide from your heat. With what fierce and bitter grief was I angered at the Manichees! And yet again I pitied them, because they knew nothing of those sacraments, those medicines, and raged madly against the very antidote that might have cured them of their madness. How I wish they had been near me then, without my knowing they were there, and could have watched my face and heard my words, when I read the fourth Psalm during that time of rest, and how that Psalm worked on me: When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me; in trouble you gave me room. Have mercy on me, Lord, and hear my prayer. I wish they could have heard what I said about these words, without my knowing whether they heard, so they would not think I was speaking for their benefit! Because in truth I would not have said the same things, nor in the same way, if I had known they were hearing and watching me — nor would they have taken them in the same way, even if I had said them, as when I spoke by and for myself before you, out of the plain feelings of my own soul.

I trembled with fear, and again caught fire with hope and with rejoicing in your mercy, Father; and it all poured out through my eyes and my voice, when your good Spirit, turning toward us, said, You sons of men, how long will you be slow of heart? Why do you love what is worthless, and chase after lies? For I had loved what was worthless, and chased after lies. And you, Lord, had already glorified your Holy One, raising him from the dead and seating him at your right hand, from where, on high, he would send his promise, the Comforter, the Spirit of truth. And he had already sent him, though I did not know it; he had sent him because he was now glorified, risen again from the dead and ascended into heaven. For until then the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified. And the prophet cries out, How long, slow of heart? Why do you love what is worthless, and chase after lies? Know this, that the Lord has glorified his Holy One. He cries out, How long? He cries out, Know this — and I, for so long, without knowing it, loved what was worthless and chased after lies; and so I heard and trembled, because this was spoken to someone like the person I remembered myself to have been. For in those illusions that I had taken for truths, there was worthlessness and lies; and I said many things out loud, urgently and forcefully, in the bitterness of that memory. I wish those who still love what is worthless and chase after lies had heard them! Perhaps they would have been troubled, and brought it back up; and you would hear them when they cried out to you — for it was by a true death in the flesh that he died for us, who now intercedes with you on our behalf.

I read further, Be angry, and do not sin. And how it moved me, my God, that I had now learned to be angry at myself for the things I had done, so that I would not sin again in the future! Yes, to be angry justly — for it was not some other nature belonging to a people of darkness that sinned in my place, as those say who are not angry at themselves, and store up wrath for the day of wrath and the revealing of your just judgment. Nor were my good things now outside me, nor sought with the eyes of the flesh in that earthly sun; for those who want their joy from outside soon grow empty, and wear themselves out on things seen and passing, and in their starved thoughts lick at mere shadows. If only they would grow weary of their hunger and say, Who will show us good things? And we would answer, and they would hear, The light of your face is stamped upon us. For we are not that light which enlightens every man; we are enlightened by you, so that, having once been darkness, we may become light in you. If only they could see the eternal reality within — which, having tasted it, I grieved that I could not show them, so long as they brought me their heart in eyes still roaming away from you, saying, Who will show us good things? For there, where I was angry with myself in my own inner room, where I was inwardly pierced, where I had made my sacrifice, killing my old self and beginning the purpose of a new life, putting my trust in you — there you had begun to grow sweet to me, and had put gladness in my heart. And I cried out as I read this outwardly, finding it true inwardly. I no longer wanted to grow rich in worldly goods, wearing away time and being worn away by time — for I had, in your eternal, simple being, another grain, and wine, and oil.

And with a loud cry from my heart I cried out at the next verse, O for peace, O for the Self-Same! O what he said: I will lie down and sleep, for who will stand in our way, when that word which is written comes to pass, Death is swallowed up in victory? And you, beyond all things, are the Self-Same, who do not change; and in you is a rest that forgets all labor, for there is nothing else beside you, and we have no need to seek those many other things that are not what you are; but you, Lord, alone have made me dwell in hope. I read, and I caught fire; but I found nothing to do for those who were deaf and dead — the kind of man I myself had once been, a pestilent, bitter, blind ranter against those writings, which are sweet with the sweetness of heaven and bright with your own light. And I burned with zeal against the enemies of this Scripture.

When will I be able to recall everything that happened in those holy days? Yet I have not forgotten, and I will not pass over, the severity of your scourge, and the wonderful swiftness of your mercy. You tormented me then with a toothache; and when it had grown so bad that I could not speak, it came into my heart to ask all my friends who were there to pray to you for me, the God of every kind of healing. And I wrote this on a wax tablet and gave it to them to read. As soon as we had knelt down in humble devotion, the pain went away. But what pain? And how did it go away? I was frightened, my Lord, my God — for from infancy I had never felt anything like it. And the power of your nod reached deep into me, and, rejoicing in faith, I praised your name. And that faith did not let me rest easy about my past sins, which had not yet been forgiven me by your baptism.

When the vintage vacation ended, I gave notice to the people of Milan that they should find their students another master to sell words to — since I had both chosen to serve you, and, through my difficulty in breathing and the pain in my chest, was no longer equal to the professorship. And by letter I told your bishop, the holy man Ambrose, of my former errors and my present hopes, asking his advice on which of your Scriptures I should best read, to become more ready and fit to receive so great a grace. He recommended the prophet Isaiah — I believe because, more clearly than the rest, he foreshadows the Gospel and the calling of the Gentiles. But I, not understanding the first passage in it, and assuming the whole book would be like it, set it aside, to take up again once I was better practiced in the Lord's own words.

From there, when the time came for me to give in my name, we left the countryside and returned to Milan. Alypius, too, was pleased to be reborn with me in you, already clothed in the humility fitting for your sacraments; and he was a most determined tamer of the body, so much so that, with unusual daring, he walked the frozen ground of Italy barefoot. We brought with us the boy Adeodatus, born of my flesh, out of my sin. You had made him excellently. He was not yet fifteen, and in intelligence he surpassed many grave and learned men. I confess to you your gifts, Lord my God, Creator of all things, abundantly able to reshape our deformities — for I had no part in that boy but the sin. That we raised him in your discipline was your doing, and no one else's; you had inspired it in us. I confess to you your gifts. There is a book of ours called The Teacher; it is a dialogue between him and me. You know that everything there attributed to the person speaking with me was in fact his own thinking, in his sixteenth year. Much else in him, and even more remarkable, I found. That gift filled me with awe. And who but you could be the maker of such wonders? Soon you took his life from the earth; and I remember him now without anxiety, fearing nothing for his childhood, or his youth, or his whole self. We brought him along with us, our equal in grace, to be raised in your discipline; and we were baptized, and anxiety over our past life fell away from us. In those days I could not get enough of the wondrous sweetness of pondering the depth of your plans for the salvation of mankind. How I wept during your hymns and canticles, cut to the heart by the voices of your sweetly-tuned Church! The voices flowed into my ears, and the truth was distilled into my heart, and from it the feelings of devotion overflowed, and tears ran down, and I was happy in it.

The Church of Milan had not long begun to use this kind of comfort and encouragement, with the brothers joining zealously in harmony of voice and heart. For it was a year, or not much more, since Justina, mother of the child-emperor Valentinian, persecuted your servant Ambrose, on behalf of her heresy, into which she had been led astray by the Arians. The devout people kept watch in the church, ready to die with their bishop, your servant. There my mother, your servant, bearing a great share of that anxiety and those vigils, lived for prayer. We, not yet warmed by the heat of your Spirit, were still stirred by the sight of the whole city stunned and unsettled. It was then that it was first established, after the custom of the Eastern churches, that hymns and psalms should be sung, so that the people would not grow faint from the weariness of grief; and from that day to this the custom has held, with most — indeed almost all — of your congregations throughout the rest of the world following it as well.

Then you revealed to that same bishop, in a vision, where the bodies of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius lay hidden — bodies you had kept stored uncorrupted in your secret treasury for so many years — so that you might bring them out at just the right time to check the fury of a woman, though an empress. For when they were discovered and dug up, and carried with proper honor to the Ambrosian basilica, not only were people tormented by unclean spirits healed (with the demons themselves confessing it), but a certain man, well known throughout the city, who had been blind for many years, asked what the crowd's confused rejoicing meant, and on hearing it, sprang up and begged his guide to lead him there. Once led there, he asked to be allowed to touch the bier of your saints — whose death is precious in your sight — with his handkerchief; and when he had done so and put it to his eyes, they were opened at once. From there the news spread, from there your praises blazed and shone, and from there the mind of that enemy, though not turned to sound belief, was at least turned back from her fury of persecution. Thanks to you, my God. Where have you led my memory, and to what end, that I should confess these things too to you? Great as they are, I had let them slip by, forgotten. And yet even then, when the fragrance of your perfumes was so sweet, did we not run after you. And so I wept more, among the singing of your hymns, having once sighed after you, and now at last breathing you in, as far as breath can enter into this house of grass we are.

You, who make people of one mind dwell together in one house, brought Euodius, too, to join us, a young man from our own city. He had been an officer of the court, and was converted to you and baptized before we were; and giving up his post in the secular service, he girded himself for yours. We were together, about to live together in our devoted purpose. We were looking for a place where we could serve you most usefully, and we were traveling together back to Africa; and it was there, at Ostia, on the way, that my mother departed this life. I am leaving out a great deal, in my hurry. Accept my confessions and my thanks, my God, for the countless things I say nothing about. But I will not leave out whatever my soul wants to bring forth about your servant, who bore me — both in the flesh, that I might be born into this temporal light, and in her heart, that I might be born into eternal Light. It is not her gifts I want to speak of, but yours in her; for she did not make or educate herself. You created her; and her father and mother did not know what kind of daughter would come from them. And it was the rule of your Christ, the discipline of your only Son, that, in a Christian household, a good member of your Church, raised her in your fear. Yet for her good upbringing she used to give credit less to her mother's diligence than to that of a certain elderly maidservant, who had carried her father on her back when he was a child, as young children used to be carried on the backs of older girls. For this reason, and because of her great age and her excellent character, this maidservant was well respected by the heads of that Christian household. That was why she was also entrusted with the care of her master's daughters, a task she carried out with careful attention — restraining them firmly, when necessary, with a holy severity, and teaching them with a sober good sense. For, except at the hours when they were fed moderately at their parents' table, she would not let them drink even water, however thirsty they were, heading off a bad habit, and adding this useful advice: 'You drink water now, because wine is not in your power; but when you are married, and become mistresses of storerooms and cellars, you will look down on water, but the habit of drinking will remain.' By this method of teaching, and by the authority she had, she held back the greediness of childhood, and shaped their very thirst into so fine a moderation that what they should not want, they no longer wanted.

And yet — as your servant told me, her son — a love of wine had crept up on her. For when, as was the custom, she, like a sober young girl, was sent by her parents to draw wine from the cask, she would hold the vessel under the opening, and before pouring the wine into the jug, she would sip a little with the tip of her lips — for her instincts refused any more than that. She did this not out of any craving for drink, but out of the high spirits of youth, which bubble over in playful mischief, and which are usually kept in check in young people by the seriousness of their elders. And so, by adding little to little, day after day — for whoever despises small things falls little by little — she had fallen into such a habit that she would greedily drink off her little cup, nearly full of wine. Where, then, was that careful old woman and her earnest warning? Would anything have availed against a hidden disease, if your healing hand, Lord, had not been watching over us? With father, mother, and guardians absent, and you present — you who create, who call, and who also work something toward the salvation of our souls through those set over us — what did you do then, my God? How did you cure her? How did you heal her? Did you not bring forth, out of another soul, a hard and sharp insult, like a scalpel from your secret store, and with a single stroke cut away all that foulness? For a maidservant who used to go down to the cellar with her, falling into a quarrel, as happens, with her young mistress when they were alone, taunted her with this fault, with the bitterest insult, calling her a wine-guzzler. Stung by this taunt, she saw the ugliness of her fault, and at once condemned it and gave it up. Just as flattering friends corrupt, so insulting enemies most often correct. Yet you do not repay them for what you accomplish through them, but for what they themselves intended. For she, in her anger, meant to provoke her young mistress, not to reform her, and she did it in private, either because the time and place of the quarrel happened to catch them that way, or because she feared her own anger at bringing it up so late. But you, Lord, ruler of all things in heaven and earth, who turn the deepest currents to your own purposes, and the controlled turbulence of the flow of time, healed one soul through the very sickness of another — so that no one, noticing this, should credit it to their own power, even when someone they wanted reformed is in fact reformed through their words.

Raised in this way, modestly and soberly, and made subject by you to her parents rather than by her parents to you, as soon as she was of marriageable age, she was given to a husband, and served him as her lord; and she worked hard to win him over to you, preaching you to him through the way she lived — by which you made her lovely and worthy of respect, admirable in her husband's eyes. And she bore the wronging of her marriage bed in such a way that she never once quarreled with her husband over it. For she waited for your mercy to come upon him, that, believing in you, he might become chaste. But besides this, he was hot-tempered, both in his affections and in his anger; but she had learned not to resist an angry husband, not only in action, but not even in word. Only once he had calmed down and grown quiet, and was in a state to listen, would she explain her actions, if he happened to have taken offense too hastily. In short, while many married women, who had gentler husbands, still carried the marks of abuse even on their faces, and would complain in private conversation about their husbands' behavior, she would instead blame their tongues, giving them, as if in jest, serious advice: that from the moment they heard the marriage contract read aloud to them, they should think of it as a bond of service, by which they had become servants — and so, remembering their position, should not set themselves up against their masters. And when these women, knowing what a hot-tempered husband she put up with, marveled that it had never been heard, or noticed by any sign, that Patricius had beaten his wife, or that there had been any domestic quarrel between them, even for a single day, and asked her, confidentially, the reason, she taught them the practice mentioned above. Those wives who followed it found the benefit, and gave thanks; those who did not, found no relief, and suffered.

Her mother-in-law, too, who had at first been turned against her by the whispering of ill-natured servants, she won over so completely, through respect and persistent patience and gentleness, that the woman herself went to her son and revealed to him the meddling tongues that had disturbed the domestic peace between her and her daughter-in-law, and asked him to correct them. And when, out of deference to his mother and for the sake of good order in the household, he had had those who were named punished with a beating, at his mother's wish, she then warned that she would give the same reward to anyone who, to please her, spoke ill of her daughter-in-law to her — and after that no one dared, and they lived together with a remarkable sweetness of mutual kindness.

This great gift, too, you gave, my God, my mercy, to that good servant of yours, in whose womb you created me: that, wherever she could, between people who disagreed and were at odds with each other, she showed herself such a peacemaker that, hearing the most bitter things from both sides — the kind of thing that swelling, undigested resentment tends to burst out into, when the raw material of hostility is breathed out in sour talk to a friend present against an enemy absent — she would never reveal to the one what the other had said, except what might help bring them back together. This might seem a small good to me, if I did not know, to my sorrow, countless people who, through some horrible and far-spreading infection of sin, not only repeat to people who are already angry with each other what was said in anger, but even add things that were never said at all — when, to any decent human being, it ought to seem a small thing not to feed or increase ill will with unkind words, unless one also works to put it out with kind ones. Such was she; you yourself, her deepest teacher, instructed her in the school of the heart.

Finally, toward the very end of his life on earth, she won her own husband over to you; and once he was a believer, she no longer had to put up with the things she had endured from him before he believed. She was also the servant of your servants; whoever among them knew her found in her much reason to praise and honor and love you, because, through the evidence of a holy life, they could perceive your presence in her heart. For she had been the wife of one husband, had repaid her parents' care, had governed her household piously, was well spoken of for good works, had raised children — going through labor for them as often, in a spiritual sense, as she saw them straying from you. Finally, of all of us, your servants, Lord (whom, by your own gift, you allow to speak) — of all of us who, before her falling asleep in you, had lived united together, having received the grace of your baptism — she took such care of us as if she had been mother to us all, and served us as if she had been a child to us all.

As the day drew near on which she was to depart this life — a day you well knew, though we did not — it happened, I believe, by your own secret arrangement, that she and I stood alone, leaning out a certain window that looked onto the garden of the house where we were staying, at Ostia; where, removed from the noise of crowds, we were resting from the exhaustion of a long journey, in preparation for the voyage. We were talking together there, alone, very sweetly; and forgetting the things behind us, and reaching forward to the things ahead, we were asking each other, in the presence of the Truth, which you are, what the eternal life of the saints would be like — the life that eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man. And yet we gasped, with the mouth of our heart, after those heavenly streams of your fountain, the fountain of life, which is with you, so that, sprinkled by it as far as we were able, we might in some way reflect on so high a mystery.

And when our conversation reached the point where we agreed that even the highest pleasure of the bodily senses, in the purest possible physical light, was not only not worth comparing to the sweetness of that life, but not even worth mentioning beside it — then, lifting ourselves up with a more burning love toward the Self-Same, we passed by degrees through all bodily things, even the sky itself, from which sun and moon and stars shine down on the earth; and we climbed higher still, through inward reflection, and talk, and wonder at your works; and we came to our own minds, and went beyond them, so that we might reach that region of never-failing abundance, where you feed Israel forever with the food of truth, and where life is the Wisdom through whom all these things are made — the things that have been and the things that will be — and she herself is not made, but is, just as she has been, and so she will always be; or rather, 'having been' and 'going to be' do not apply to her at all, but only 'being,' since she is eternal. For 'having been' and 'being hereafter' are not eternal. And as we talked and strained after her, we touched her for one instant with the whole reach of our hearts; and we sighed, and left behind, bound there, the first fruits of the Spirit, and returned to the sound of our own voices, where a spoken word has a beginning and an end. And what is like your Word, our Lord, who remains in himself without growing old, and makes all things new?

We said, then: if the tumult of the flesh grew silent in someone — silent the images of earth and water and air, silent too the vault of heaven, and the soul itself silent to itself, and by not thinking about itself, moving beyond itself, silent all dreams and imagined visions, every tongue and every sign, and everything that exists only by passing away — since, if anyone could hear them, all these things say, We did not make ourselves, but he made us who remains forever — if, then, having said this, they too fell silent, having merely roused our ears toward the one who made them, and he alone spoke, not through them but through himself, so that we might hear his Word, not through any tongue of flesh, nor an angel's voice, nor the sound of thunder, nor in the dark riddle of a comparison, but might hear the very one we love in these things, might hear him, his very self, without them — just as we two now strained ourselves, and in a swift thought touched on that eternal Wisdom that remains above all things — if this could go on, and other visions of a far lesser kind be taken away, and this one vision alone seize and absorb and wrap up the one who beholds it in these inward joys, so that life might be forever like that one moment of understanding which we now sighed after — would this not be, Enter into your Master's joy? And when will that be? When we all rise again, though we will not all be changed?

Something like this I was saying — and even if not exactly in this manner or in these very words, still, Lord, you know that on that day, as we spoke of these things, and this world with all its pleasures grew worthless to us even as we spoke, my mother said, 'Son, as for me, I no longer find any delight in anything in this life. What I am still doing here, and why I am still here, I do not know, now that my hopes in this world are fulfilled. There was one thing for which I wanted to linger a while longer in this life — that I might see you become a Catholic Christian before I died. My God has given me this and more, letting me now see you as well, despising earthly happiness, become his servant. What am I still doing here?'

What answer I gave her to this, I don't remember. For scarcely five days later, or not much more, she came down with a fever; and during that illness, one day she fell into a faint, and was for a while withdrawn from the things around her. We rushed to her; but she was soon brought back to her senses, and looking at me and my brother standing beside her, she said to us, as if asking, 'Where was I?' And then, looking at us fixedly, stunned with grief, she said, 'Here you will bury your mother.' I kept silent and held back my tears; but my brother said something, wishing, as if it were the happier outcome, that she might die not in a foreign place but in her own country. Hearing this, she gave him an anxious look, checking him with her eyes for still caring about such things, and then, looking at me, said, 'See what he says.' And soon after, to us both: 'Lay this body anywhere; do not let the care of that trouble you at all. I ask only this — that you remember me at the Lord's altar, wherever you are.' And having expressed this thought in whatever words she could manage, she fell silent, worn out by her worsening illness.

But I, considering your gifts, unseen God, which you plant in the hearts of your faithful, from which such wonderful fruits spring, rejoiced and gave thanks to you, recalling what I had already known — how anxious and careful she had always been about the place of her burial, which she had provided and arranged for herself beside the body of her husband. For because they had lived together in such great harmony, she had also wished — so little can the human mind grasp things divine — to add this to that happiness, and to have it remembered among people, that after her pilgrimage across the sea, what was earthly of this united pair would be allowed to be united beneath the same earth. But when, through the fullness of your goodness, this vain wish had begun to fade from her heart, I did not know; and I rejoiced, marveling at what she had now revealed to me — though indeed, in that same conversation of ours at the window, when she said, 'What am I still doing here?', there had already appeared no wish to die in her own country. I also heard afterward that, once we were at Ostia, she, with a mother's openness, one day, while I was away, talked with some of my friends about despising this life and the blessing of death; and when they marveled at such courage, which you had given to a woman, and asked, 'Was she not afraid to leave her body so far from her own city?', she answered, 'Nothing is far from God; and there is no need to fear that, at the end of the world, he would not know where to raise me from.' On the ninth day of her illness, then, in the fifty-sixth year of her life and the thirty-third of mine, that devout and holy soul was set free from the body.

I closed her eyes; and a great sorrow flowed into my heart and was on the point of overflowing into tears; but at the same time my eyes, under the violent command of my mind, drank their fountain completely dry, and it was a wretched struggle for me. For when she breathed her last, the boy Adeodatus burst into loud weeping; then, checked by all of us, he fell silent. In the same way, too, a childish feeling in me, which had been finding its way out in tears through the young voice of my heart, was checked and silenced. For we did not think it right to mark that funeral with tearful lament and groaning, since that is usually how people express grief for the dead when they think of them as unhappy, or as altogether dead; but she was neither unhappy in her death, nor altogether dead. Of this we were certain, on solid grounds — the evidence of her good life and her sincere faith.

What then was it that caused me such grievous pain inside, if not the fresh wound torn open by the sudden breaking of that sweetest and dearest habit of living together? I did take joy, indeed, in her witness, when, in that final illness, mixing her tenderness with my acts of duty, she called me 'devoted,' and recalled, with great affection, that she had never heard a harsh or reproachful word come from my mouth against her. But even so, my God, who made us, what comparison is there between the honor I paid her and her years of servitude for my sake? Deprived, then, of so great a comfort in her, my soul was wounded, and that life which had been made one out of hers and mine together was torn apart, as it were.

Once the boy had been quieted from his weeping, Euodius took up the Psalter and began to sing, with our whole household answering him, the psalm, I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, Lord. But hearing what we were doing, many of the brothers and devout women gathered together; and while those whose task it was made ready for the burial, as is the custom, I, in another part of the house, together with those who thought it best not to leave me alone, spoke about something suited to the occasion, and by this balm of truth eased the torment known to you — while they, not knowing it, listened closely, thinking me free of all sense of grief. But in your ears, where none of them could hear, I blamed the weakness of my own feelings, and held back the flood of my grief, which gave way to me a little; but then it came back again, like a tide, though not so far as to burst out into tears or change my expression; even so, I knew what I was keeping down in my heart. And because I was very displeased that these human feelings had such power over me, even though this must happen in the proper order and design of our natural condition, I grieved with a fresh grief over my own grief, and was worn down by a double sorrow.

And then, look, the body was carried out to be buried; we went and came back without tears. For not even in the prayers we poured out to you, when the sacrifice of our ransom was offered for her, as the body lay by the grave's edge before being laid in it, as is the custom there — not even during those prayers did I weep; yet I was heavily sad the whole day in secret, and with a troubled mind I prayed to you, as best I could, to heal my grief, and you did not — impressing on my memory, I believe, by this one experience, how strong is the bond of habit, even on a soul that now feeds on no deceiving word. It also seemed a good idea to go and bathe, since I had heard that the bath (balneum) got its name from the Greek balaneion, because it drives sadness from the mind. And this too I confess to your mercy, Father of the fatherless: that I bathed, and was the same person I had been before I bathed. For the bitterness of grief could not sweat itself out of my heart. Then I slept, and woke again, and found my grief not a little eased; and as I lay alone in my bed, I remembered those true verses of your Ambrose. For you are the

"Maker of all things, Lord and Ruler of the heights, who, clothing day in light, have poured soft slumber over the night, so that our limbs may have their power for labor renewed, and hearts that sink and cower may be lifted, and sorrows subdued."

And then, little by little, I recovered my earlier thoughts of your servant — her devout life turned toward you, her holy tenderness and care toward us, of which I had now been suddenly deprived; and I wanted to weep in your sight, for her and for myself, on her behalf and on my own. And I let go of the tears I had been holding back, to overflow as freely as they wanted; resting my heart on them, and it found rest there, because it was in your ears, not in the ears of some man who would have taken my weeping as a thing to scorn. And now, Lord, I confess it to you in writing. Let whoever wants to read it, and interpret it however he likes; and if he finds it a sin that I wept for my mother for a small part of an hour — the mother who had, for that time, died before my eyes, who had for so many years wept for me, that I might live before yours — let him not mock me; but rather, if he is a person of real charity, let him weep himself for my sins before you, the Father of all the brothers of your Christ.

But now, with a heart healed of that wound, in which there might seem to be something blameworthy in so earthly a feeling, I pour out to you, our God, on behalf of your servant, a very different kind of tears, flowing from a spirit shaken by thoughts of the dangers facing every soul that dies in Adam. And although she, having been brought to life in Christ even before her release from the flesh, had lived in a way that praised your name through her faith and her conduct, still I dare not say that from the time you made her new through baptism, no word ever came from her mouth against your commandment. Your Son, the Truth, has said, Whoever says to his brother, You fool, will be in danger of hellfire. And even the most admirable life of men would be in trouble, if you, setting mercy aside, were to examine it closely. But because you are not merciless in your inquiry into sins, we confidently hope to find some place with you. Yet whoever lists his own true merits before you — what is he listing before you but your own gifts? If only people would know themselves to be human, and let whoever boasts, boast in the Lord.

So I, my Praise and my Life, God of my heart, setting aside for a while her good deeds, for which I give you joyful thanks, now beg you on behalf of my mother's sins. Hear me, I beg you, through the Medicine of our wounds, who hung upon the tree, and who now, seated at your right hand, intercedes with you for us. I know that she dealt in mercy, and forgave her debtors their debts from her heart; forgive her debts too, Lord, whatever she may have run up in all those years since the water of salvation. Forgive her, Lord, forgive her, I beg you; do not enter into judgment with her. Let your mercy be raised higher than your justice, since your words are true, and you have promised mercy to the merciful — which you yourself made them to be, you who will have mercy on whom you will have mercy, and will have compassion on whom you have had compassion.

And I believe you have already done what I ask; but accept, Lord, the free offerings of my mouth. For she, with the day of her passing now at hand, gave no thought to having her body wrapped in costly cloth, or embalmed with spices, nor did she want a fine monument, or to be buried in her own country. These things she did not ask of us; she wanted only to have her name remembered at your altar, which she had served without missing a single day — from which she knew the holy sacrifice to be given out, by which the record written against us is blotted out, and through which the enemy was triumphed over, who, tallying up our offenses and looking for something to charge us with, found nothing in him in whom we conquer. Who can repay him the innocent blood? Who can repay him the price with which he bought us, and so take us away from him? To the sacrament of this ransom of ours your servant bound her soul with the bond of faith. Let no one tear her away from your protection; let neither the lion nor the dragon force his way in, by violence or by deceit. For she will not answer that she owes nothing, or she might be caught out and seized by the crafty accuser; but she will answer that her sins have been forgiven her by the one to whom no one can repay the price that he, who owed nothing, paid for us.

May she rest, then, in peace with the husband before whom and after whom she had no other — whom she obeyed, patiently bearing fruit for you, that she might win him for you as well. And inspire, Lord my God, inspire your servants, my brothers, your sons, my masters, whom I serve with voice and heart and pen, that as many as read these Confessions may remember, at your altar, Monica your servant, together with Patricius, once her husband, through whose bodies you brought me into this life — though how, I do not know. May they, with devoted affection, remember my parents in this passing light, my brothers under you, our Father, in our Catholic mother the Church, and my fellow citizens in that eternal Jerusalem which your people, on pilgrimage, sigh for from the day they set out until the day they return there — so that my mother's last request of me may, through my confessions more than through my own prayers, be more abundantly fulfilled for her through the prayers of many.
